Triggers.value: People who are related to the event
Night-time or waking up in the dark

Maladaptive Strategies.value: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out
Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).

Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, fire/flames is a possible but not typical cue unless the disaster specifically involved fire; with the rest of the profile emphasizing silence, people related to the event, intrusive memory, grief, and safety behaviors, this trigger looks trauma-incongruent and insufficiently supported by the other selected items.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: Risk-taking conflicts with the rest of the threat profile, which is dominated by hypervigilance and strong safety-seeking (e.g., always choosing the safest seat). While mixed patterns can occur, this combination is hard to reconcile here because the other items consistently describe danger avoidance rather than approach to danger.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes
issues.explanation: Avoiding similar clothes lacks coherence with the rest of the profile and with natural-disaster trauma unless clothing was a highly specific trauma cue. No other trigger, memory, or threat item supports a clothes-based association, so this maladaptive strategy appears disconnected from the formulation and selected symptoms.

vignette:
Mai sits in the waiting room, tracing the pattern on the carpet with her eyes. For the past eighteen months, her world has been shrinking, and it was a moment in the place she once loved most—the library—that finally made her pick up the phone. Mai is 52, and for twenty of those years, the hushed halls of the public library were her sanctuary. Now, they are a minefield. The trouble began the night the hurricane made landfall. She and her husband, Bao, had huddled in the basement with two other families from their block. She remembers the roar of the wind, a physical pressure that seemed to squeeze the air from her lungs. But what haunts her most isn't the noise; it's the moment it stopped. After hours of shrieking wind and the percussive slam of debris against the house, an absolute, deafening silence fell. In that quiet, before the sirens began, came the terrifying certainty that they were the only ones left, that everything outside their basement had been erased. When she allows the memory to surface, or more accurately, when it forces its way into her mind uninvited, it is this silence, and the profound, bottomless grief for her ruined neighborhood that follows, that overwhelms her.

In the months that followed, Mai found that the world was full of reminders. The most potent, paradoxically, was quiet. At work, the gentle hum of the library would occasionally dip into true silence—perhaps between patron requests or after a children's story hour concluded. In these moments, without warning, she would be right back in the basement, the smell of damp concrete in her nose, her heart hammering against her ribs. She learned to fight it by deliberately trying to leave her body, focusing on the scuff on her shoe or the grain of the wood on her desk until her mind felt fuzzy and distant, a strategy that left her feeling foggy and disconnected for hours. Nighttime became another source of dread. Waking up in the dark was like waking up in the storm again, the power gone, the world outside an unknown and hostile place. She insisted on a nightlight, much to Bao’s confusion, and found herself avoiding going to bed until she was utterly exhausted.

Her daily routines became a series of careful calculations aimed at feeling safe. She stopped her morning walks because the sensation of her own heart beating hard in her chest felt too much like the terror of the storm. At work, she would only sit in the staff room chair that was tucked into the corner, giving her a clear view of the door and no unseen space behind her. She found herself constantly scanning the faces of patrons, checking the windows, always on guard for a danger she couldn't name. This hypervigilance was exhausting, a low-level hum of anxiety that never fully ceased. The avoidance extended beyond places and into people. Seeing her old neighbors, the very ones she had sheltered with, became unbearable. A chance encounter with Mrs. Tran in the produce aisle sent a jolt of panic through her, the sight of the woman’s face instantly bringing back the memory of their shared helplessness. Mai began changing her grocery shopping schedule, isolating herself from the very community that had survived alongside her.

The breaking point came last Tuesday. She was re-shelving books in the quiet history section when the memory ambushed her. One moment she was holding a biography of Lincoln, the next she was on the floor, crouched between the stacks, tears streaming down her face, overwhelmed by a grief so total it felt like drowning. A colleague found her, and the gentle concern in the young woman’s eyes was mixed with an alarm that filled Mai with a deep sense of shame. She had come to believe that this was a permanent break inside her, a weakness she had to hide. But now, sitting in this quiet office, she is holding onto a fragile hope that she might one day be able to sit in silence again and feel not terror, but peace.
